questions.stem: About the diffusion coefficient of a solute in a membrane, Dm = D(1 − σ)·Sp/S, the correct propositions are:
options: Dm is the diffusion coefficient of the solute in the membrane
Sp is the area of the permeable pores only
Dm is greater than D because the membrane channels the solute
The diffusive flux can be written Jd = +Dm·dC/dx (no minus sign)
questions.explanation: Dm = D(1 − σ)Sp/S is the solute's diffusion coefficient in the membrane, and Jd = −Dm·dC/dx. Sp is the total pore area (permeable and impermeable). Because (1 − σ) ≤ 1 and Sp/S < 1, Dm is smaller than D, and it is zero when σ = 1.

questions.stem: About the diffusive permeability P of a membrane, the correct propositions are:
options: The initial diffusive flux is Jdᵢ = P·|ΔCᵢ|
P is proportional to the membrane thickness l
questions.explanation: P = (D/l)(S′/S) = Dm/l, in m/s (not m²/s, which is the unit of D). Since l is in the denominator, P is inversely proportional to the thickness. From Jdᵢ = Qᵢ/S = P|ΔCᵢ| you get P = Qᵢ/(S|ΔCᵢ|).

questions.stem: About the relation D = kT/f, the correct propositions are:
options: f is the friction coefficient of the solvent on the diffusing particles
For spherical particles of radius r, f = 6πηr
questions.explanation: D = kT/f, where k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J/K and f is the solvent's friction on the particles (f = 6πηr for spheres). Because f is in the denominator, more friction means a smaller D. The lesson's worked answers give D in m²/s.

questions.stem: For spherical particles, D = Cste·(T/η)·(ρ/M)^(1/3). The correct propositions are:
options: D is inversely proportional to the cube root of the molar mass M
D is proportional to the density ρ
Doubling the viscosity of the solvent doubles D
The particle radius is r = Cste·(M/ρ)^(1/3)
questions.explanation: From M = 𝒩ρ(4/3)πr³, r = Cste·(M/ρ)^(1/3). Then D = kT/(6πηr) is proportional to T/η and to (ρ/M)^(1/3). So D varies with the cube root of ρ, not with ρ itself, and it is halved, not doubled, when η doubles.

questions.stem: Two spherical proteins A and B have the same density and are in the same solvent at the same temperature. B's molar mass is 8 times A's. B's diffusion coefficient is:
questions.explanation: D ∝ (ρ/M)^(1/3) at fixed T and η, so D_B = D_A·(1/8)^(1/3) = D_A/2. A heavier particle diffuses more slowly, never faster, and the dependence is a cube root, not a square root.

questions.stem: A spherical particle has D = 6 × 10⁻¹¹ m²/s in a solvent of viscosity 1 mPa·s at 300 K. At the same temperature, in a solvent of viscosity 1.5 mPa·s, its diffusion coefficient becomes:
questions.explanation: D = kT/(6πηr) is inversely proportional to η: 6 × 10⁻¹¹ / 1.5 = 4 × 10⁻¹¹ m²/s. Multiplying by 1.5 instead of dividing gives 9 × 10⁻¹¹, and treating the effect as a cube root gives 5.2 × 10⁻¹¹.

questions.stem: A spherical macromolecule has a diffusion coefficient D = 2 × 10⁻¹¹ m²/s in water at 27°C (η = 10⁻³ Pa·s; k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J/K). Its radius is approximately:
questions.explanation: r = kT/(6πηD) = (1.38 × 10⁻²³ × 300)/(6π × 10⁻³ × 2 × 10⁻¹¹) ≈ 1.1 × 10⁻⁸ m = 11 nm. Using 273 K instead of 300 K gives 10 nm, and leaving out the 6 gives 66 nm.

questions.stem: Two aqueous solutions of the same solute, 40 mmol/L and 100 mmol/L, are separated by a dialysis membrane with a total area of 5 cm². The initial molar flow rate of the solute is 9 pmol/s. The diffusive permeability of the membrane (in 10⁻⁹ m/s) is:
questions.explanation: P = Qᵢ/(S|ΔCᵢ|) = 9 × 10⁻¹² / (5 × 10⁻⁴ × 60) = 0.3 × 10⁻⁹ m/s (60 mmol/L = 60 mol/m³). Using the sum of the concentrations (140) gives 0.13, and using only 40 gives 0.45.

questions.stem: (Continued: P = 0.3 × 10⁻⁹ m/s.) The membrane is 20 µm thick, its pores make up 2% of its total area, and σ = 0. The diffusion coefficient D of the solute is:
questions.explanation: With σ = 0, P = (D/l)(Sp/S), so D = P·l·S/Sp = 0.3 × 10⁻⁹ × 20 × 10⁻⁶ / 0.02 = 3 × 10⁻¹³ m²/s. Forgetting the pore fraction gives 6 × 10⁻¹⁵, multiplying by it gives 1.2 × 10⁻¹⁶, and forgetting l gives 1.5 × 10⁻⁸.

questions.stem: Two glucose solutions, 0.5 mol/L and 0.2 mol/L, are separated by a dialysis membrane with an area of 10 cm². The membrane's diffusive permeability to glucose is 4 × 10⁻⁶ m/s. The initial molar flow rate is:
questions.explanation: Qᵢ = P·S·|ΔCᵢ| = 4 × 10⁻⁶ × 10 × 10⁻⁴ × 0.3 × 10³ = 1.2 × 10⁻⁶ mol/s = 1.2 µmol/s. Concentrations must be converted from mol/L to mol/m³ (× 10³); forgetting that gives 1.2 × 10⁻³, and using the sum (0.7) gives 2.8.

questions.stem: An artificial kidney has a diffusion surface S = 1 m² and an average pore length l = 40 µm. The dialysate is constantly renewed and free of urea. The diffusion coefficient of urea in the membrane is Dm = 8 × 10⁻¹⁰ m²/s. For an initial blood urea concentration of 2 g/L, the initial mass flow rate of urea is:
questions.explanation: Qᵢ = (Dm·S/l)·|ΔCᵢ| with |ΔCᵢ| = C₀ − 0 = 2 g/L = 2 × 10³ g/m³. So Qᵢ = (8 × 10⁻¹⁰ × 1 / 40 × 10⁻⁶) × 2 × 10³ = 4 × 10⁻² g/s = 40 mg/s.

questions.stem: In the artificial-kidney calculation (blood at C₁ᵢ = C₀; dialysate constantly renewed, so C₂ᵢ = 0), the correct propositions are:
options: Because the dialysate is urea-free, Qᵢ does not depend on the pore length
Doubling the diffusion surface S halves Qᵢ
questions.explanation: Qᵢ = P·S·|ΔCᵢ| = (Dm·S/l)·|ΔCᵢ|, and |ΔCᵢ| = C₀ − 0 = C₀ because the dialysate is urea-free. Qᵢ is proportional to S and inversely proportional to l; a urea-free dialysate only sets ΔCᵢ.

questions.stem: The initial molar flow rate of a solute across a dialysis membrane is Qᵢ = P·S·|ΔCᵢ|, with P = Dm/l. Which changes, each made alone, double Qᵢ?
options: Doubling the total membrane area while keeping the same pore fraction Sp/S
Doubling the viscosity of the solvent
questions.explanation: Qᵢ is proportional to |ΔCᵢ| and S, and P = Dm/l is inversely proportional to l, so halving l doubles Qᵢ. Doubling S at a fixed pore fraction leaves P unchanged and doubles Qᵢ. Doubling η halves D (D = kT/6πηr), so it halves Qᵢ.

questions.stem: About dialysis and hemodialysis, the correct propositions are:
options: In medicine, dialysis purifies the blood of its waste products (urea, creatinine, excess potassium or liquid) across a membrane
In hemodialysis, the exchanges take place inside the body
In hemodialysis, the artificial filter is called a dialyzer
The fluid that exchanges with the blood is called the dialysate
Peritoneal dialysis uses an artificial filter placed outside the body
questions.explanation: Hemodialysis exchanges take place outside the body, between the blood and the dialysate, through an artificial filter called a dialyzer. Peritoneal dialysis takes place inside the body, across the peritoneum.

questions.stem: The figure shows a dialysis technique (one label has been hidden). The correct propositions are:
options: The exchanges between the blood and the dialysate take place inside the body
The membrane used is the peritoneum, a richly vascularized membrane that envelops the abdominal organs and the digestive tract
The blood flows through an external dialyzer
The dialysate is placed in the abdominal cavity
questions.explanation: This is peritoneal dialysis: dialysate is run into the abdominal cavity and exchanges with the blood inside the body, across the peritoneum. Hemodialysis instead sends the blood to an external dialyzer.
